subject: Critical Thinking
title: No True Scotsman: Moving the Goalposts
description: A quick, practical guide to No True Scotsman: Moving the Goalposts.

hook.text: 'No Scotsman puts sugar in his porridge.' 'Angus does.' 'Well, no TRUE Scotsman puts sugar in his porridge.'

buildup.text: No True Scotsman: redefining a group to exclude counterexamples rather than accepting that the claim was wrong.

twist.text: You see it everywhere: 'Real Christians don't do that.' 'A true patriot would never...' The definition shifts to win.

punchline.text: If you keep changing the definition, you aren't making an argument.

quiz.question: What is the 'No True Scotsman' fallacy?
options: Redefining a group to exclude counterexamples rather than accepting the claim was wrong

details.summary: No True Scotsman protects a generalization by retroactively redefining the group to exclude counterexamples. When shown a Scottish criminal, one says 'No true Scotsman would do that,' shielding the claim from any possible refutation.
details.whyItMatters: This fallacy makes claims unfalsifiable by quietly changing definitions to exclude inconvenient evidence, shutting down productive debate.
takeaways: Counterexamples are dismissed by redefining group membership
The original claim becomes unfalsifiable through ad hoc exclusion
The name comes from a thought experiment by Antony Flew

faq.question: How can you tell if someone is using the No True Scotsman fallacy?
faq.answer: After a counterexample is presented, they add qualifications that were not in the original claim. If 'all Xs do Y' becomes 'all real Xs do Y' only after a counterexample appeared, the goalposts have moved.

faq.question: Is it ever legitimate to refine a definition in response to counterexamples?
faq.answer: Yes, if the refinement is based on genuine criteria established independently. The fallacy occurs when the sole purpose of the redefinition is to exclude the inconvenient example, with no independent justification.
